body_markdown:
Iron supplements are commonly recommended for people with iron deficiency or iron deficiency anaemia, but taking an iron tablet is not always as simple as swallowing it with whatever drink or meal happens to be nearby.


A medical education expert has highlighted how certain foods, drinks and other supplements can affect the way iron is absorbed by the body. The advice is particularly useful for people who experience unpleasant side effects from iron tablets or are unsure about the best time to take them.


Iron is an important mineral that the body needs to make haemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body. When iron levels become too low, people can develop iron deficiency anaemia, which may cause symptoms such as tiredness, weakness, headaches, shortness of breath and difficulty concentrating.


However, not everyone who feels tired necessarily has an iron deficiency. Iron deficiency can have several causes, including blood loss and problems affecting absorption. This is why experts advise getting the underlying cause investigated rather than simply starting supplements because of unexplained tiredness.


## Why iron tablets can be difficult to tolerate


Iron supplements are well known for causing digestive problems in some people. Common side effects can include nausea, constipation, diarrhoea and stomach discomfort.


For this reason, there can be a difficult balance between taking iron in a way that maximises absorption and taking it in a way that allows you to tolerate the treatment.


Iron is generally absorbed more effectively when taken on an empty stomach. However, taking it without food can make stomach-related side effects worse for some people.


If an iron supplement repeatedly causes nausea or other digestive symptoms, taking it with or after food may make treatment easier to tolerate. Consistently taking a slightly less absorbable dose is generally more useful than repeatedly missing doses because the supplement makes you feel unwell.


People should follow the instructions provided with their particular iron preparation, as recommendations can vary depending on the product.


## Coffee could interfere with iron absorption


One of the biggest points highlighted by Professor Rachel Woods, an Associate Professor of Medical Education at the University of Nottingham and University of Lincoln, concerns coffee.


Coffee contains compounds that can interfere with the absorption of iron. According to evidence discussed by Woods, coffee consumed alongside an iron supplement substantially reduced iron absorption in a small study involving women with depleted iron levels.


The study found that taking coffee with a 100mg iron supplement reduced absorption compared with taking the supplement with water.


This does not necessarily mean coffee has to be completely removed from your diet. Instead, it may be sensible to avoid taking an iron supplement at the same time as coffee, particularly if you have been advised to take iron to correct a deficiency.


The same principle can apply to other drinks and foods that may influence mineral absorption, so checking the instructions for your specific supplement is worthwhile.


## What about vitamin C?


Vitamin C is often mentioned alongside iron because it can increase iron absorption.


Research discussed by Woods found that 80mg of vitamin C increased iron absorption by around 30 percent in one study. However, taking a much larger amount did not appear to provide additional benefits.


Importantly, improved absorption does not always translate into better treatment outcomes.


A randomised trial involving hundreds of adults with iron deficiency anaemia found that iron alone was similarly effective to iron combined with vitamin C when it came to improving haemoglobin and iron stores.


This means people should not automatically assume that they need a high-dose vitamin C supplement whenever they take iron.


For many people, following the instructions given by their healthcare professional is more important than trying to create the perfect combination of supplements.


## Calcium supplements may need separating


Another issue involves calcium.


Calcium can reduce iron absorption when the two are taken together, particularly when relatively large amounts are consumed at the same time.


However, evidence suggests that the effect on long-term iron status may be relatively small. This means the situation is not necessarily as straightforward as saying that calcium and iron can never be taken on the same day.


If you have been advised to take both calcium and iron supplements, it is sensible to ask a pharmacist or healthcare professional whether they should be taken at different times.


This is particularly important if you are taking several supplements or prescription medicines, as the timing of one product can sometimes affect another.


## Does the time of day matter?


There has also been interest in whether iron should always be taken in the morning.


Some research suggests iron absorption may be higher earlier in the day. One study mentioned by Woods found absorption was lower in the afternoon compared with the morning.


However, the difference was not strong enough to establish a firm rule that everyone should take iron in the morning.


In practical terms, the best time may depend on your individual circumstances, your specific supplement and whether taking it at a particular time causes stomach problems.


The most important thing is usually taking the supplement consistently according to the instructions you have been given.


## Avoid taking more than you need


Iron is an essential mineral, but more is not necessarily better.


People sometimes take several supplements at the same time without having been advised to do so. High doses of certain vitamins and minerals can cause harm, and excessive intake of some substances can lead to toxicity.


Iron supplements should therefore not be treated like an ordinary wellness product that everyone needs.


If you suspect you have low iron because you feel tired or run down, speak with a healthcare professional rather than automatically starting high-dose supplements. Blood tests can help establish whether iron deficiency is present and whether further investigation is needed to determine why.


This is particularly important because iron deficiency can sometimes be linked to blood loss or conditions affecting the digestive system.


## The simple takeaway


If you have been prescribed or advised to take iron, pay attention to what you take alongside it.


Coffee may reduce iron absorption, while vitamin C can increase absorption in some circumstances. Calcium may also interfere with absorption when taken at the same time.


At the same time, taking iron on an empty stomach can cause digestive side effects. If nausea, constipation, diarrhoea or stomach pain makes treatment difficult, taking the supplement with food may make it easier to continue.


Rather than trying to optimise every detail yourself, follow the instructions for your particular iron preparation and ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are also taking other medicines or supplements.


The goal is not simply to maximise the amount of iron absorbed from one tablet. The goal is to correct the deficiency safely and consistently while addressing the reason your iron levels became low in the first place.


### Our Final Word


Iron supplements can be helpful when they are genuinely needed, but taking them correctly matters. Simple habits, such as avoiding coffee around the time of your dose and checking whether calcium or other supplements should be separated, may help you get the most from your treatment. Most importantly, iron deficiency should be properly assessed rather than self-diagnosed based on tiredness alone.


### Disclaimer


This article is for general information and educational purposes only. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Do not start, stop or change an iron supplement without appropriate medical or pharmacy advice, particularly if you have been diagnosed with anaemia, take other medicines or have an underlying health condition. If you experience persistent or severe symptoms, seek advice from a qualified healthcare professional.
